key_terms.meaning: A rule that assigns exactly one output f(x) to each input x in the domain; written f: A → B.
Domain = set of allowed inputs; range = set of outputs actually produced.
The set of all points (x, f(x)) drawn in the xy-plane.
(f∘g)(x) = f(g(x)), defined only where x is in the domain of g and g(x) is in the domain of f.
f⁻¹ undoes f: f⁻¹(f(x)) = x; it exists when f is one-to-one on its domain.
lim(x→a) f(x) = L means f(x) can be made as close to L as we like by taking x close to a, with x ≠ a.
lim(x→a⁻) f(x) uses only x < a; lim(x→a⁺) f(x) uses only x > a; the two-sided limit exists only when both exist and are equal.
f is continuous at a when f(a) is defined, lim(x→a) f(x) exists, and the limit equals f(a).
[f(x+h) − f(x)]/h, the slope of the secant line through x and x+h; h ≠ 0.
f′(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h) − f(x)]/h, the slope of the tangent, where this limit exists.
If f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b) and f(a) = f(b), then some c in (a,b) has f′(c) = 0.
If f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), some c in (a,b) has f′(c) = [f(b) − f(a)]/(b−a).
Pₙ(x) = Σ(k=0 to n) f⁽ᵏ⁾(a) (x−a)ᵏ / k!, the degree-n polynomial matching f and its first n derivatives at a.
Rₙ(x) = f(x) − Pₙ(x) = f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(c)(x−a)ⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)! for some c between a and x.
A limit that first reads as 0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞, ∞−∞, 1^∞, 0⁰ or ∞⁰; the value is not fixed by the form alone.
For 0/0 or ∞/∞, lim f(x)/g(x) = lim f′(x)/g′(x), provided the second limit exists (finite or infinite).
A point c in the domain where f′(c) = 0 or f′(c) does not exist.
If f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) > 0 then c is a local minimum; if f″(c) < 0 then c is a local maximum; if f″(c) = 0 the test gives no answer.
f is concave up where f″ > 0 (graph bends upward) and concave down where f″ < 0.
A point where the concavity of f changes sign; often f″ = 0 there, but f″ = 0 alone is not enough.

takeaways: A function gives exactly one output per allowed input, and every new function built by shifting, stretching, composing or inverting keeps that rule.
A limit describes the value f approaches near a point, not the value at the point, so f(a) may be missing or different and the limit can still exist.
Continuity at a point is three conditions in one line: f(a) exists, the limit exists, and the two are equal.
The derivative is itself a function, produced by taking the limit of the difference quotient; differentiability at a point forces continuity there.
Rolle's theorem is the flat-tangent case of the mean value theorem, and the mean value theorem turns information about f′ into information about f.
Taylor's theorem replaces a smooth function near a point by a polynomial plus a remainder, and the remainder controls how large the error can be.
L'Hôpital's rule converts a 0/0 or ∞/∞ limit into a new limit of derivatives, and it is valid only when that new limit exists.
Derivatives find the critical points; a sign test on f′ or the value of f″ at the critical point classifies them, and on a closed interval the endpoints must also be checked.
The sign of f″ decides where the graph bends up or down, and a change of that sign marks an inflection point.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit usually ask you to state a theorem with all its hypotheses, draw the picture that explains it, and then verify it on a specific function or use it to prove an inequality or an estimate.

bank.q: State the ε–δ definition of lim(x→a) f(x) = L. Use it to prove that lim(x→3) (2x + 1) = 7, showing clearly how δ is chosen for a given ε.
outline: Correct ε–δ statement with 0 < |x − a| < δ ⇒ |f(x) − L| < ε
Work backwards from |2x + 1 − 7| = 2|x − 3|
Choose δ = ε/2 and write the forward verification
Mention that the point x = 3 itself is excluded

bank.q: Define continuity of a function at a point and on an interval. Explain the three types of discontinuity (removable, jump, infinite) with one example of each, and state the intermediate value theorem.
outline: Definition: f(a) defined, limit exists, limit equals f(a)
Interval continuity: continuous at every point of the interval
Examples: (x²−1)/(x−1) at 1; |x|/x at 0; 1/x at 0
Correct classification and sketches
Statement of the intermediate value theorem with continuity on [a,b]

bank.q: State Rolle's theorem and Lagrange's mean value theorem. Give the geometric meaning of each and show by counterexample that each hypothesis is necessary.
outline: Both statements with continuity on [a,b] and differentiability on (a,b)
Rolle needs f(a) = f(b)
Geometric meaning: horizontal tangent; tangent parallel to the chord
Counterexample for continuity: f(x) = 1/x on [−1,1] or a step function
Counterexample for differentiability: f(x) = |x| on [−1,1]
Counterexample for f(a) = f(b) in Rolle: f(x) = x on [0,1]

bank.q: Define the derivative of f at a point as a limit. Show that differentiability at a point implies continuity there, and give an example of a function that is continuous but not differentiable at a point.
outline: f′(a) = lim(h→0) [f(a+h) − f(a)]/h
Proof: f(a+h) − f(a) = h × (difference quotient) → 0
Correct limit algebra and conclusion f(a+h) → f(a)
Example f(x) = |x| at 0 with left and right difference quotients 1 and −1
Note the converse fails

bank.q: State Taylor's theorem with the Lagrange form of the remainder. Write the Maclaurin expansions, with remainder, of eˣ, sin x and log(1 + x).
outline: f(x) = Pₙ(x) + Rₙ(x) with Pₙ built from derivatives at a
Correct remainder formula with c between a and x
eˣ = 1 + x + x²/2! + … + xⁿ/n! + e^c xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)!
sin x expansion with alternating signs and odd powers
log(1 + x) expansion and its interval of validity |x| < 1
Note Maclaurin is Taylor with a = 0

bank.q: Evaluate: (a) lim(x→0) sin 3x / tan 5x, (b) lim(x→0) (1 − cos x)/x², (c) lim(x→∞) (√(x² + x) − x).
outline: (a) Use sin θ/θ → 1 and tan θ/θ → 1; answer 3/5
(b) Either 1 − cos x = 2 sin²(x/2) or one use of L'Hôpital; answer 1/2
(c) Multiply by the conjugate (√(x² + x) + x) and divide by x; answer 1/2
Each step justified by a limit law, not by substituting the point

bank.q: Use L'Hôpital's rule to evaluate (a) lim(x→0) (eˣ − 1 − x)/x², (b) lim(x→0⁺) x log x, (c) lim(x→∞) (log x)/x^(1/3).
outline: Identify the form before each use: 0/0, 0·(−∞), ∞/∞
(b) Rewrite x log x as log x / (1/x) to reach ∞/∞
(c) One application gives (1/x)/((1/3)x^(−2/3)) → 0
Answers: 1/2, 0, 0
State that the rule is applied only while the form is indeterminate

bank.q: For f(x) = x³ − 3x² + 1 on the interval [−1, 4], find all critical points, classify them, and give the absolute maximum and minimum values on that interval.
outline: f′(x) = 3x² − 6x = 3x(x − 2); critical points x = 0 and x = 2, both in the interval
Second derivative f″(x) = 6x − 6: local max at 0 (value 1), local min at 2 (value −3)
Evaluate f at endpoints: f(−1) = −3, f(4) = 17
Compare all four values: absolute maximum 17 at x = 4, absolute minimum −3 at x = 2 and x = −1
Statement that endpoints must be tested on a closed interval

bank.q: Verify Rolle's theorem for f(x) = x² − 4x + 3 on [1, 3], and verify the mean value theorem for f(x) = x³ − x on [0, 2] by finding the value of c in each case.
outline: Check continuity on the closed interval and differentiability on the open interval
Check f(1) = f(3) = 0 for Rolle
Solve f′(c) = 0: c = 2 in (1,3)
For MVT compute [f(2) − f(0)]/(2 − 0) = 3
Solve 3c² − 1 = 3 giving c = 2/√3, which lies in (0,2)

bank.q: Find the Taylor polynomial of degree 3 for f(x) = √x about a = 4. Use it to estimate √4.2 and bound the error using the Lagrange remainder.
outline: Substitute x = 4.2 for the estimate
Remainder |R₃| = |f⁗(c)| |0.2|⁴/4! with f⁗(x) = −15/(16 x^(7/2)); bound on [4, 4.2] using x = 4
State the numerical answer with the error bound

bank.q: Find the constant k so that the piecewise function f(x) = x² + k for x ≤ 1 and f(x) = 3x − 1 for x > 1 is continuous at x = 1. Then examine whether it is differentiable at x = 1 for that k.
outline: Left limit 1 + k, right limit 2, f(1) = 1 + k
Continuity forces k = 1
Left derivative 2x → 2, right derivative 3
The two one-sided derivatives differ, so f is not differentiable at 1 although continuous
Comment: continuity does not imply differentiability

bank.q: For f(x) = x/(1 + x²), find the intervals of increase and decrease, the local extrema, the concavity intervals and the inflection points, then sketch the graph.
outline: f′(x) = (1 − x²)/(1 + x²)²; critical points x = ±1
Increasing on (−1,1), decreasing outside
Local minimum −1/2 at x = −1, local maximum 1/2 at x = 1
f″(x) = 2x(x² − 3)/(1 + x²)³; sign changes at x = 0 and x = ±√3
Concave up on (−√3,0) and (√3,∞); inflection points at x = 0, ±√3
Sketch with horizontal asymptote y = 0

bank.q: Using the mean value theorem, prove that |sin a − sin b| ≤ |a − b| for all real a and b, and that x/(1 + x) < log(1 + x) < x for x > 0.
outline: Apply MVT to sin x on the interval between a and b
|sin a − sin b| = |cos c| |a − b| ≤ |a − b|
Apply MVT to log(1 + t) on [0, x]
log(1 + x) = x/(1 + c) for some c in (0, x)
Use 0 < c < x to get 1/(1 + x) < 1/(1 + c) < 1
Multiply by x > 0 to finish both inequalities

bank.q: State L'Hôpital's rule precisely, including its hypotheses. Explain with the example f(x) = x + sin x, g(x) = x why the rule cannot be applied blindly at infinity, and give a case where f′/g′ has no limit while f/g does.
outline: Statement for 0/0 and for ∞/∞, with the requirement that lim f′/g′ exists
Emphasise the hypothesis is on the new limit, not the old one
For (x + sin x)/x, f′/g′ = 1 + cos x, which has no limit as x → ∞
Yet f/g = 1 + (sin x)/x → 1
Conclusion: the rule is a one-way implication, and failure of f′/g′ proves nothing
Note also that applying the rule when the form is not indeterminate gives wrong answers

bank.q: A closed cylindrical can of volume 500 cm³ is to be made from sheet metal. Find the radius and height that minimise the total surface area, and justify that your answer is a minimum.
outline: Let r be the radius, h the height; V = πr²h = 500 gives h = 500/(πr²)
Surface S = 2πr² + 2πrh = 2πr² + 1000/r
dS/dr = 4πr − 1000/r² = 0 gives r³ = 250/π
h = 2r, so the can is as tall as its diameter
Justify minimum: d²S/dr² = 4π + 2000/r³ > 0 for r > 0
Give the numerical radius with units

glossary.def: The largest value f(c) taken by f on its whole domain or on a stated interval.
A line that the graph of a function approaches without necessarily meeting, either as x → ±∞ or as f(x) → ±∞.
The function f∘g defined by (f∘g)(x) = f(g(x)) wherever both steps are defined.
A graph shape where f″ > 0, so the curve lies above its tangent lines and slopes increase.
The state where f(a) is defined, lim(x→a) f(x) exists, and the two are equal.
A point c in the domain of f where f′(c) = 0 or f′(c) fails to exist.
The function f′ whose value at x is the limit of the difference quotient, giving the slope of the tangent.
Having a derivative at the point, that is, the difference quotient has a finite two-sided limit there.
The ratio [f(x+h) − f(x)]/h, the slope of a secant line, whose limit is the derivative.
A point where continuity fails; removable if the limit exists, jump if one-sided limits differ, infinite if the function blows up.
The set of all inputs for which the function rule is defined.
A function continuous on a closed interval [a,b] attains both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum there.
An expression such as 0/0 or ∞/∞ whose limiting value depends on the functions, not on the form.
A point on a curve where the direction of concavity changes.
The function f⁻¹ that sends each output of a one-to-one f back to its input.
The value L that f(x) approaches as x approaches a, regardless of the value at a itself.
A value f(c) that is at least as large as f(x) for all x in some open interval around c.
The theorem that a differentiable curve has a tangent parallel to the chord joining its endpoints somewhere in between.
The limit computed using only x on one side of the point, written lim(x→a⁻) or lim(x→a⁺).
A function defined by different formulas on different parts of its domain.
The set of all values actually taken by the function.
The difference f(x) − Pₙ(x) between a function and its Taylor polynomial, which measures the error of the approximation.
The special case of the mean value theorem in which the two endpoint values are equal, so some interior derivative is zero.
The polynomial of degree n that matches f and its first n derivatives at a chosen point.
